data.title: CUPE warns province-wide CAS layoffs are putting children, families and frontline workers at risk
data.description:
CUPE warns province-wide CAS layoffs are putting children, families and frontline workers at risk

More than 800 positions lost as Children’s Aid Societies struggle with inadequate provincial funding

More than 800 positions have been lost across Children’s Aid Societies (CAS) in Ontario between 2019 and 2025, and CUPE is warning that continued layoffs and unfilled vacancies are leaving frontline workers struggling to support vulnerable children and families.

CUPE represents more than 4,000 frontline workers at 26 CAS agencies across the province. Based on information gathered from CUPE locals in the sector, CUPE estimates staffing has declined by 17 per cent across its CAS bargaining units.

The cuts are being felt across the province. Catholic Children’s Aid Society of Hamilton reduced its workforce from 120 employees in 2023 to just 70 this year. Peel CAS cut 30 contract positions in 2026, while London and Middlesex Children’s Aid Society has experienced a net loss of 47 frontline staff since 2024. In Durham Region, 10 staff left through voluntary exit options and early retirement in 2025, and their positions were not replaced.

“Children’s Aid workers are being asked to do more with less, while the needs of children and families continue to grow,” said Yolanda McClean, President of CUPE Ontario. “These are not just numbers on a budget sheet. Every position lost means less capacity to support a family in crisis, respond to a child’s needs and keep children safe. The Ford government cannot continue to underfund child welfare and ignore the consequences.”

For frontline workers, the impact is immediate. Fewer staff means heavier caseloads, more pressure and less time to provide the support children and families need. Workers are also facing increased administrative demands, making it even harder to keep up with their responsibilities.

“When positions are cut and people aren’t replaced, the work doesn’t disappear – it gets handed to the workers who are left,” said Kelly Dwyer, a Children’s Aid worker in Durham Region. “Our caseloads keep growing, and we’re expected to meet the same demands with fewer people and less time. We do everything we can for the children and families we serve, but it becomes harder every day to give them the attention and support they deserve.”

CUPE estimates that when a child protection worker is not replaced, between 15 and 25 children or families may be left to be supported by colleagues who already have full caseloads.

The union has written directly to the Minister of Children, Community and Social Services to raise the alarm about layoffs and unfilled positions. The recent release of the government’s review of Children’s Aid Societies has also reinforced what frontline workers have been saying: the system is underfunded, workers are struggling to do their jobs, and children and families are at risk.

CUPE estimates that real per-capita funding for Children’s Aid Societies has fallen by 20.3 per cent since 2018. The 2026 provincial budget also includes a planned 2.4 per cent reduction in real per-capita funding for social services.

“Doug Ford’s government has had years to address this crisis, but instead, funding continues to fall behind while frontline positions disappear,” said McClean. “The government must stop treating child welfare as an expense to be cut. It has a responsibility to ensure Children’s Aid Societies have the resources and staff they need to protect children and support families.”

CUPE is calling on the provincial government to:

  • Restore funding to Children’s Aid Societies and rebuild frontline staffing.
  • Approve new licences and expand safe placements and housing for vulnerable children.
  • Reverse the decision to stop tracking deaths of children who have interacted with the child welfare system.

“Children and families cannot wait for this government to act,” McClean said.

data.title: Apollo and Goldman Sachs Announce Pricing of $44 Billion SpaceX GPU Financing
data.description:
Transaction was led by Apollo and Goldman Sachs Alongside Leading Global Investors

NEW YORK, Nov. 20, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Apollo (NYSE: APO) and Goldman Sachs (NYSE: GS) today announced the successful pricing of approximately $44 billion of senior and subordinated notes to fund the purchase of GPUs and related equipment for SpaceX (NASDAQ: SPCX). The transaction, which was oversubscribed and upsized as a result of strong investor demand, will deliver the next generation of NVIDIA Vera Rubin chips for SpaceX’s terrestrial compute buildout and represents the largest GPU financing executed to date. Lease schedules are expected to commence upon delivery of GPUs and related equipment in the first half of 2027.

Financing was committed by funds and affiliates managed by Apollo and Goldman Sachs, with funds and accounts managed by BlackRock, Goldman Sachs Asset Management and capital accounts advised by KKR providing anchor commitments in the transaction. Apollo Global Securities and Goldman Sachs served as Co-Global Coordinators, while Goldman Sachs served as Sole Structuring Agent.

“SpaceX is one of the most ambitious builders of compute in the world, and we are pleased to have led this financing alongside Goldman Sachs,” said Apollo Partner Jamshid Ehsani. “This transaction reflects the strength of Apollo’s integrated platform, where origination, structuring, syndication and principal investing work together to deliver flexible capital at scale. It also reflects our focus on downside-protected, asset-based structures.”

Apollo was advised by Morgan Stanley, Citi and PJT Partners on the transaction. 

Latham & Watkins LLP served as legal counsel to Apollo. Paul, Weiss, Rifkind, Wharton & Garrison LLP served as investor counsel.

data.title: Investors fled to healthcare stocks for safety. Now insurance and hospital shares are plunging.
data.description:
By Jaimy Lee

Shares of UnitedHealth, Humana and CVS Health declined this week in light of a new Medicare for All proposal

Hospital and health-insurance stocks fell this week after the government announced plans to crack down on healthcare fraud and Sen. Bernie Sanders revealed a new Medicare for All proposal.

Are healthcare stocks like UnitedHealth Group really the safe bet that investors fleeing the AI trade expect them to be?

That's the big question this week after several health insurance and hospital companies plunged over worries about regulatory threats to their businesses, including a fresh Medicare for All proposal and a government-initiated crackdown on Medicare Advantage health-insurance fraud.

Over the past five days, shares of UnitedHealth (UNH) fell 16.6%, Humana (HUM) dropped 14.2%, and those of CVS Health (CVS) are down 9.1%. The Community Health Systems (CYH) hospital system plunged 26.5%, while Tenet Healthcare (THC) - another large hospital system - is trading about 9.3% lower.

Even Hims & Hers Health (HIMS) fell 19% during a week in which the telehealth company launched a highly anticipated business selling compounded peptides to the American public.

As of Friday morning trading, the State Street Health Care Select Sector SPDR Exchange-Traded Fund XLV declined slightly more this week - 5.8% - than the broader S&P 500 SPX, which is down 5.4%.

At face value, the health-insurance and hospital stocks face serious threats to their businesses.

The shift in power in Washington opened the door to a Democratic healthcare agenda, including a new Medicare for All proposal from Sen. Bernie Sanders, an independent from Vermont, that would lower the age of Medicare eligibility to 55 and add dental, vision and hearing coverage to traditional Medicare. The incremental changes appear more realistic than a full immediate transition to a single-payer health system - and could hurt insurers that already offer Medicare Advantage plans.

But analysts are skeptical that Medicare for All will pan out.

"With no clear Democratic consensus around replacing private insurance, significant legislative hurdles under President [Donald] Trump and no guarantee that the 2028 election produces a more favorable path for Medicare for All, we believe the risk currently reflected in managed care valuations is greater than the probability of the policy ultimately becoming law," wrote Mizuho Securities analyst Ann Hynes in a note.

Industry experts know that issues like this cyclically pop up for healthcare companies, which are heavily regulated by the government, which is also the largest contributor to their revenue. But healthcare policy proposals are often intertwined with politics.

"It's a movie we've seen before and feels all too familiar from the 2019-2020 Democratic primary cycle, when [Medicare for All] concerns peaked as Bernie Sanders and Elizabeth Warren ran for president," Barclays analyst Andrew Mok told investors this week. "While the headline risk is real, the practicality is not."

-Jaimy Lee

data.title: GREENROW OPENS NEW STORE IN PALO ALTO
data.description:
GREENROW OPENS NEW STORE IN PALO ALTO

New Retail Location Located in Town & Country Village Brings GreenRow’s Inspired, Sustainable Design to California’s South Bay Area

GreenRow, a portfolio brand of Williams-Sonoma, Inc. (NYSE: WSM), the world’s largest digital-first, design-led and sustainable home retailer, announced today the opening of the brand’s second retail store located at Town & Country Village in Palo Alto, California. The new Palo Alto location follows GreenRow’s debut flagship store in New York City’s SoHo neighborhood, which opened earlier this year and was recently named one of House Beautiful’s “Best Home Stores in America.”

Launched in 2023, GreenRow offers thoughtfully designed home furnishings made with an emphasis on craftsmanship, responsible sourcing, and lower-impact production. The brand prioritizes innovative manufacturing practices and low-impact materials wherever possible, while supporting at least one of Williams-Sonoma, Inc.’s social or environmental initiatives. Responsibly sourced linen, cotton, wood, and recycled materials are featured throughout the assortment, along with handmade and artisanal pieces that showcase the unique qualities of their materials and craftsmanship.

The GreenRow Palo Alto store’s assortment of furniture, lighting, textiles, rugs, tabletop, and décor showcases the brand’s belief that sustainability should not require a compromise in style, comfort or individuality. Products featured in the store are designed to bring warmth, character and style to every room in the home in a responsible and considered way. Customers who visit the new store can also shop a curated collection of vintage, found and one-of-a-kind pieces, while receiving complimentary design services and personalized guidance from GreenRow’s design experts.

“Our stores are a destination for inspiration and a place where customers can explore beautiful products, learn more about the materials behind them to help curate a home that feels both personal and purposeful,” said Jaimee Seabury, Vice President of GreenRow. “We look forward to welcoming the South Bay Area community into a space that showcases GreenRow’s commitment to craftsmanship, creativity and making sustainable design more accessible, inspiring and relevant to everyday life.”

To celebrate the new store opening, GreenRow will host a grand opening weekend from Friday, November 20, through Sunday, November 22, 2026. The celebration will be open to the public, and a portion of net proceeds from opening weekend sales will be donated to Filoli Historic House & Garden.

For more information about GreenRow or the new Palo Alto store, please visit: www.GreenRow.com.

GreenRow Palo Alto
Town & Country Village, 855 El Camino Real, Suite 10, Palo Alto, CA 94301

ABOUT GREENROW

GreenRow is a mission-driven home furnishings brand that creates modern heirlooms that balance beauty, comfort, and integrity—proving that design can be aspirational and responsibly made. Every product in the GreenRow assortment supports at least one of Williams-Sonoma, Inc.’s social or environmental initiatives and is made using innovative, low-impact manufacturing practices wherever possible. The collections showcase a commitment to craftsmanship and prioritize responsibly sourced materials—including linen, cotton, wood, and recycled fibers—selected for their quality, durability, and reduced environmental impact.

ABOUT WILLIAMS-SONOMA, INC.

Williams-Sonoma, Inc. (NYSE: WSM), a Fortune 500 and S&P 500 company, is the world’s largest digital-first, design-led and sustainable home retailer. The company’s brands — Williams Sonoma, Pottery Barn, Pottery Barn Kids, Pottery Barn Teen, West Elm, Williams Sonoma Home, Rejuvenation, Mark & Graham, GreenRow, and Dormify — represent distinct merchandise strategies that are marketed through e-commerce, direct-mail catalogs, retail stores, and business-to-business. data.title: Global Survey Uncovers an "Aloneware" Crisis: Isolated AI Development Threatens Enterprise Stability and Adds Maintenance Costs
data.description:
Global Survey Uncovers an "Aloneware" Crisis: Isolated AI Development Threatens Enterprise Stability and Adds Maintenance Costs

Global Survey Uncovers an "Aloneware" Crisis: Isolated AI Development Threatens Enterprise Stability and Adds Maintenance Costs

PR Newswire

MCLEAN, Va., Nov. 20, 2026

Two-thirds of AI decision-makers and IT leaders say standalone coding assistants lead to "aloneware": software that's difficult to support, understand, and maintain.

MCLEAN, Va., Nov. 20, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Appian (Nasdaq: APPN), an AI automation leader, today released new research asking AI decision-makers and IT leaders about AI-assisted development. They found that enterprise investments in fast-tracked AI software development are creating an unexpected drain on corporate innovation capital, with 82% of enterprise leaders allocating at least 10% of their current technology innovation funds to test, deploy, maintain, update, integrate, and/or repair isolated AI software builds.

Enterprise investments in AI software development are creating an unexpected drain on corporate innovation capital.

In the global survey of 851 respondents at large enterprises, Appian defines a new term: "aloneware." These are applications built or modified with AI-assisted development tools outside an approved enterprise platform environment. While these tools accelerate initial code creation, organizations face mounting friction to understand AI-generated applications and keep them functional, secure, and integrated over time.

Upfront speed creates downstream work

Initial build speed is failing to deliver long-term efficiency. Just over seven in 10 (71%1) enterprise leaders surveyed report that while standalone AI tools accelerate development, they are spending more time across testing, system integration, troubleshooting, scaling, and/or deployment.

According to Matt Calkins, CEO of Appian, "Some people get so excited about 'free' software that they forget the risks. Enterprises can now create tech debt faster than ever before."

Aloneware diverts strategic innovation budgets

The operational burden of maintaining software built outside a platform is directly diverting capital away from strategic growth. More than eight in 10 (82%) enterprise leaders surveyed report allocating at least 10% of their current technology innovation budgets to testing, deploying, maintaining, updating, integrating, and/or repairing software built outside a platform environment. And 43% of those surveyed currently allocate at least 20% of the budget—a figure that 64% expect to allocate within the next two years, indicating that the financial drain is accelerating quickly.

Compounding these budget demands, more than two-thirds (68%2) of enterprise leaders report unexpected post-launch costs or resources tied directly to security, governance, and compliance remediation.

The support void and the need for platforms

When isolated AI applications break, organizations face a critical support void. More than two-thirds (68%3) of leaders find it challenging to access accountable technical support when problems arise with applications built outside a platform, while 66%3 report difficulties keeping code, architecture, dependencies, and system integrations up to date.

Against this backdrop, 73%4 of respondents state that a shared architectural foundation would improve their ability to control total cost of ownership and 71%4 say it would help them maintain software over time.

"The most important applications in enterprises need support," Calkins adds. "If you vibe-code them, there will be nobody to turn to when problems occur. Using AI to build applications on a commercial platform combines the speed of AI with the reliability of supported technology."

To access the complete research findings and executive report, visit appian.com/aloneware.

About the research

The research was conducted by Censuswide among 851 senior decision-makers who primarily work in AI/Engineering or IT, work at large enterprises (5,000 employees or more, or annual revenue exceeding $1 billion), and who work on at least three software systems annually. Respondents were based in Australia, the USA, New Zealand, France, Germany, Italy, Spain and the UK. Data was collected between 21 and 30 October 2026.

Censuswide is a member of the Market Research Society (MRS) and the British Polling Council (BPC), and a signatory of the Global Data Quality Pledge. The research adheres to the MRS Code of Conduct and ESOMAR principles.

  1. 'Completely agree' and 'Mostly agree' responses combined
  2. 'Significant additional cost or resource' and 'Some additional cost or resource' responses combined
  3. 'Very challenging' and 'Somewhat challenging' responses combined
  4. 'Improve significantly' and 'Improve somewhat' responses combined

About Appian

Appian provides AI automation for the most important business processes at the world's largest organizations.  

On the Appian Platform, customers build AI-powered processes that accelerate work, reduce cost, and manage risk. Our platform is known for its unique power, reliability, and scale. We've been automating processes for more than 25 years and have proven expertise in enterprise operations. For more information, visit appian.com. [Nasdaq: APPN]

data.title: Consumer Sentiment Climbed in November
data.description:
By Matt Grossman

Consumer sentiment improved in November, according to the University of Michigan's monthly survey, yet it remains near historically low levels that reflect Americans' widespread economic frustrations.

The survey's sentiment index ended November at 51.5, a rise from 48 in October. That also was an improvement from the preliminary November reading of 51 published earlier this month.

Stock-market volatility dented the mood among wealthier Americans who own more assets, said Joanne Hsu, the survey's director. By contract, sentiment improved among low- and middle-wealth consumers.

Democrats and independents reported brighter economic expectations after this month's blue-wave midterm elections rebuked Republicans' economic stewardship. Republicans reported a decline in economic expectations.
